quick.lead: Pick two archetypes, and a Title idea for each if you like.
quick.more: Each archetype has a mechanic, something only it can do, and on most of them 1 Aura adds +2 to one die on it. You can take the same archetype twice, and then that +2 is a +3. Every Title idea says which archetypes it suits, and gives you Titles, permissions and traits to start from. See How archetypes work.

quick.lead: Write a Title for each, and three permissions on it.
quick.more: Your Title is the name you give your archetype. Take one of the idea’s examples or write your own, and make it specific: the best blade in the city is fine, and the best blade in the Low Market is better. Then take three permissions that fit inside it, so you’ve got six. Change the words to suit your character, or write one that isn’t on the list. A permission can be one word, like Deceptive, or a doing word and how, what or where, like pick a mechanical lock. See Titles and Permissions.
A trait’s never a step, so it does its one thing without going on a set action. Take them from the ideas you started from, or from the full list.

Defend, Fight, Move, Sneak, Study and Talk are on every sheet, and if there’s something you do all the time, give it a set action of its own. Put your Titles on every set action they fit nearly every time, each permission on the two it helps most, never twice on the same one, and each plain item on the one it helps most. Plain armour, a shield and a helmet go on your Defend. A set action’s steps are 1 for the action and 1 for every line on it. See Set actions.

quick.lead: Take what you carry, and attune one thing.
quick.more: You carry 3 equipment, 3 utility items and a keepsake, and your bag holds 10 more. Armour, a shield or a helmet is Common, with 1 box, and one piece can be Fine, with 2. Your attuned thing starts at Awakened with one permission. If there’s trouble you’d like on it, give it a Catch and it gets a second permission. You can attune more later, in downtime. See What you carry and Attunement.

Answer at least two of the ten crew questions, and turn two of your answers into bond threads with the crew, something good between you. A thread with someone in the crew goes on both your sheets, so agree on it together. Write a hostile thread as well, with anyone, and you can write a third bond thread. With two players, one of your bond threads goes to someone outside the crew, and playing alone, both do. See Bonds and threads.

It’s one thing you want, and it climbs as you chase it. Past d12 you get it, so make it something you’d know the day it’s done: be a hero again is too vague, and earn back the rank they stripped from me is better. See Aspiration and A good Aspiration.

You’ve got 5 Aura, 2 Resolve (one for each Title), a stride of 3 and a wound die at d2. Confidence starts every scene on d6, a size up in clothes that fit the scene, and a trait like Iron Will can start you higher. Then it swings a size at a time: up when you win a roll or stop a telegraph, and down when you’re hurt or miss with every die. See Resolve, Wounds and Confidence.

traits.name: Unyielding
traits.html: The first Hurt you take each scene doesn’t move your wound die.

traits.name: Battle Focus
traits.html: The first time your Aura runs out each scene, gain 3 Aura.

traits.name: Killer Instinct
traits.html: Gain 1 Aura when you take a threat down.

traits.name: Duelist
traits.html: When you’re fighting someone one-on-one, you win ties without paying Aura.

traits.name: Pack Fighter
traits.html: When a friend’s action and yours go into the same roll, it wins ties without paying Aura.

traits.name: Never Unarmed
traits.html: You’ve always got a knife hidden on you, whatever anyone searched.

traits.name: Marksman’s Eye
traits.html: If you haven’t moved this round, your shots win ties without paying Aura.

traits.name: Ready Hand
traits.html: Once a round, pulling something out of your bag costs no action.

traits.name: Tenacious
traits.html: The first time each scene a Hurt would make you Blaze, it doesn’t, and your wound die stays at d12.

traits.name: Field Dressing
traits.html: Your first quick heal each scene costs no Aura.

traits.name: Healer’s Hands
traits.html: Your quick heals cost no Aura, once a scene for each person, yourself included.

traits.name: Tend the Crew
traits.html: When a scene you were in ends, everyone in the crew who was in it rolls two Confidence dice for their rest, and the best counts.

traits.name: Predator’s Eye
traits.html: The first time you go at a threat each scene, the GM tells you whether it’s got a weak point, and where.

traits.name: Light on my Feet
traits.html: +2 units of movement per round.

traits.name: Sure-Footed
traits.html: Ignore difficult ground.

traits.name: Fast
traits.html: In the first round of every scene, you get a Move action that costs no action.

traits.name: Acrobatic
traits.html: The first time you fall each scene, it’s a safe landing, and you move 3 units straight after.

traits.name: Silent Step
traits.html: Coming out of hiding gives you 1 Aura, as well as your extra action.

traits.name: Sprinter
traits.html: When you take a Move action, your stride counts twice that round.

traits.name: Nimble
traits.html: Grabbed and Pinned fade two sizes a round on you, not one.

traits.name: Second Wind
traits.html: The first time your wound die steps up each scene, you get an extra action.

traits.name: Lucky
traits.html: The first time each scene you roll a 1 on one of your own dice, roll it again.

traits.name: Focused
traits.html: On your first roll each scene, your lowest die counts as its highest face. It isn’t a top face, so there’s no Aura for it.

traits.name: Reputation Precedes Me
traits.html: In a scene where people know who you are, you start a size up on Confidence.

traits.name: Silver Tongue
traits.html: The first social roll you fail each scene succeeds anyway.

traits.name: Charming
traits.html: The first time each scene you win a social roll against someone you haven’t got a bond with, you’ve got a bond thread with them for the scene.

traits.name: Commanding Presence
traits.html: Anyone who answers to you follows your orders without a roll, unless the order would get them killed.

traits.name: Cold Reader
traits.html: The first time you speak with someone in a scene, the GM tells you their mood in a word.

traits.name: Style
traits.html: Clothes that fit the scene start you two sizes up on Confidence, not one.

traits.name: Showstopper
traits.html: While a crowd’s watching you, a friend in it can go into hiding without a roll.

traits.name: Intimidating Presence
traits.html: When you’re threatening someone, you win ties without paying Aura.

traits.name: Diplomat
traits.html: Two sides about to fight always hear you out first, so nobody starts it before you’ve had your say.

traits.name: Host
traits.html: Every downtime, someone you’ve hosted owes you a small favour.

traits.name: Iron Will
traits.html: You start every scene a size up on Confidence.

traits.name: Steady Hands
traits.html: Being shaken doesn’t stop you: at d2 you can still act at what the scene’s about without spending Resolve.

traits.name: Hard to Lie To
traits.html: The first time each scene someone lies to your face, the GM tells you it’s a lie.

traits.name: Perfect Recall
traits.html: You remember everything you’ve seen and heard, and the GM tells you anything from a scene you were in, exactly as it was.

traits.name: Quick Study
traits.html: The first time you face a threat each scene, the GM tells you one of its hidden tags.

traits.name: Cool Under Pressure
traits.html: The first time you’re shaken each scene, your Confidence comes straight back to where it started the scene.

traits.name: Deep Well
traits.html: Your Aura maximum is one higher.

traits.name: I Have the Thing
traits.html: Your bag’s always got the plain utility item you need. Pulling it out still takes your action, and you cross off a purse of gold for it.

traits.name: Prepared
traits.html: You can carry one more utility item.

traits.name: Cache
traits.html: At the start of every downtime, take any plain item you like from your stash, equipment or utility.

traits.name: Tireless
traits.html: You get three downtime slots, not two.

traits.name: Scout Ahead
traits.html: The first scene each session in a place you’ve seen before has 3 more ground tags, ones you spotted last time.

traits.name: Network
traits.html: When you take it, write 3 new bond threads, on bonds you’ve already got.

traits.name: Tactical Mind
traits.html: The first time you look a place over each scene, the GM tells you one useful thing about it that nobody else has noticed.

conditions.passive: One step less on fighting with what was in your hand.
conditions.active: it’s gone: out of reach, or in their hand. Cross it off until you get it back.

conditions.name: Blinded
conditions.passive: One step less on anything that needs your eyes.
conditions.active: one of your dice this round goes wide: it doesn’t count.

conditions.name: Deafened
conditions.passive: One step less on anything that needs your ears.
conditions.active: you can’t join a friend’s roll, or have a friend join yours, this round.

conditions.name: Silenced
conditions.passive: One step less on anything spoken.
conditions.active: you can’t speak this round: no orders, no words of power, no talking your way out.

conditions.name: Frightened
conditions.passive: One step less on anything that brings you closer to what you fear.
conditions.active: your next action goes on getting away from it.

conditions.name: Shaken
conditions.passive: One step less on your Confidence.
conditions.active: your Confidence steps down one size.

conditions.name: Stunned
conditions.passive: One step less on everything.
conditions.active: you can’t answer telegraphs this round.

conditions.name: Taunted
conditions.passive: One step less on anything not aimed at whoever taunted you.
conditions.active: your next action has to go at them.

conditions.name: Charmed
conditions.passive: One step less on anything against whoever charmed you.
conditions.active: you do one thing they ask. A player can refuse, and steps Confidence down one size instead.

conditions.name: Spotted
conditions.passive: One step less on hiding, and getting away.
conditions.active: whoever spotted you learns one thing: where you are right now, or one of your hidden tags.

conditions.name: Hexed
conditions.passive: One step less on one kind of thing, named when it’s placed.
conditions.active: one roll you just won becomes a tie.

conditions.name: Hunted
conditions.passive: One step less on hiding, and resting.
conditions.active: a clock ticks: they’re closing in.

conditions.name: Warded
conditions.passive: One step more on your Defend.
conditions.active: it takes a Hurt instead of you.

conditions.name: Heartened
conditions.passive: One step more on your Confidence.
conditions.active: your Confidence comes back up a size, as far as where it started the scene.

conditions.name: Covered
conditions.passive: One step more on your Defend, while whoever covers you is close.
conditions.active: a blow meant for you lands on them instead, and they choose where.

conditions.name: Braced
conditions.passive: One step more on holding your ground.
conditions.active: nothing moves you, pins you or knocks you down this round.

conditions.name: Unseen
conditions.passive: One step more on anything done unnoticed.
conditions.active: take an extra action.

conditions.name: Fleet
conditions.passive: One step more on moving.
conditions.active: move your stride again, free, whenever you like this round.

conditions.name: Blessed
conditions.passive: One step more on the action it blesses.
conditions.active: if that action fails, roll it again.

conditions.name: Inspired
conditions.passive: One step more on one of your set actions, named when it’s placed.
conditions.active: gain 1 Aura.

conditions.name: Rallied
conditions.passive: One step more on answering telegraphs.
conditions.active: answer one telegraph without spending an action.

conditions.name: Sighted
conditions.passive: One step more on anything against one target.
conditions.active: the GM tells you one of its hidden tags.

conditions.name: Guided
conditions.passive: One step more on finding your way.
conditions.active: bring the ground in without paying Aura.

conditions.name: Disguised
conditions.passive: One step more on passing as someone else.
conditions.active: one person believes it completely. No roll.

conditions.name: Fortunate
conditions.passive: One step more on anything that’s mostly chance.
conditions.active: win a tie without paying Aura.

conditions.name: Surging
conditions.passive: One step more on one of your set actions, named when it’s placed.
conditions.active: one of its dice becomes a d12 before you roll.

s-round.title: The Round
s-round.html:
1. The GM telegraphs. Everything that’s coming this round goes on the table, face up: what it’s doing, who it’s aimed at, and how hard, in dice.
  2. The players act, in any order they like, one action each. You can spend yours answering one telegraph, put it into a friend’s answer, or spend it on something else, like going at a threat or working a stake. Talk it through and make a plan. There’s no initiative.
  3. The round ends. Every telegraph nobody answered lands. Clocks and events nobody worked step down, and every condition steps down one size. Then the GM telegraphs the next round.

Everything else in this chapter is what happens inside a round.

s-telegraphs.title: Telegraphs
s-telegraphs.html:
A telegraph is the GM saying out loud what’s about to happen, before anything’s rolled. It always tells you three things:

  • What it’s doing (its intent). Pin Bram against the wall. Slip up the stair to wake the house. Slam the vault door.
  • Who or what it’s aimed at: a character, several characters, a stake or a place.
  • How hard (its dice). A d10.

s-answering.title: Answering a Telegraph
s-answering.html:
To answer a telegraph, spend your action and build a roll from the set action that fits the way you’re stopping it: dodge it, parry it, shove the brute’s arm aside, shout the crowd down, slam the door before it slams on you, or shoot the archer first. Then roll against the telegraph’s dice. Friends can put their actions in too, and then it’s a combo with one roll between you.

  • Win, and it’s stopped. It doesn’t land.
  • Lose, and it lands at once, right there and then, and nobody rolls a defence against it. A tie’s a loss, unless you pay 1 Aura.

Answering’s a gamble. It lets you throw everything you’ve got at a problem instead of trusting your Defend, but if the answer fails, you’ve walked straight into it. Your Confidence rides on it too, the same as any action. Win and it goes up a size, once, even though it’s a telegraph stopped as well. If every die you rolled misses, it drops a size, on top of whatever the telegraph costs you when it lands.

  • You can answer for someone else. Get your shield in front of the spear, drag your friend out of the way, or talk over the man shouting at her. If you answered by putting yourself in the way and you lose, it lands on you. If you’d rather it came at you, intercept it instead.
  • Several dice on the same answer are advantage: your best die counts.
  • Taking the source down answers everything it telegraphed. If the archer falls before the end of the round, his arrow never flies. Strip a tag and whatever it gave a telegraph goes with it, so if you take its Reach, the spear can’t reach you.
  • Telegraphs aimed at a stake, a place or a clock have no defence to roll. If nobody answers them, they happen.

s-the-roll.title: The Roll
s-the-roll.html:
Most of the time you’re rolling against something that pushes back: a guard, a lock, a magistrate, a storm. You roll your dice, you roll theirs too in another colour, and you compare. The GM almost never touches a die in Zi’Dara. She’s busy running everything else.

  • Beat it and you did it.
  • Tie and it goes to whoever’s defending: you when something lands on your Defend or Confidence, him when you go at the guard. If you’re the one acting, even to stop something coming at you, you can pay 1 Aura to win the tie. The GM never spends Aura, and there’s no Aura in downtime (see Downtime).
  • Roll under and you didn’t. Try something else, or spend 1 Resolve to roll again (see Resolve).

A target rolls its defence once a round. The first time anyone goes at a threat in a round, roll its die, and that roll stands against everyone who goes at it till the round’s over. It’s different for you when the telegraphs land: you roll your Defend once and your Confidence once, and each die stops one telegraph (see When It Lands). Spend your action to Defend and the lines on your Defend count twice, so you’ve got more dice to stop blows with. Your Confidence rolls as it is.

Your Confidence moves with the dice. It starts every scene on d6. It goes up a size for every action where one of your dice wins and for every telegraph your defence stops, and it drops a size for every action where all your dice miss and every time your wound die steps up. At d2 you’re shaken, and at d12 you’re fired up (see Confidence).

A wall you need to climb or a book you’ve got to get through before dawn doesn’t fight back, but it’s still a Challenge, and you still roll its die and have to beat it. A Challenge is a die twice its number, so Challenge 2 is a d4 and Challenge 6 is a d12. Threats have tags too, like Armoured or Loyal, and your wins strip them off. A win can also leave a condition, like Burning, that carries your die. Both are in Conflict.

Whenever one of your dice rolls its highest number, its top face, you get 1 Aura back. Every die counts on its own, area dice included. A die your archetype’s +2 took to its top face, or past it, doesn’t give you Aura, and nor does a number an Oracle swapped in. Small dice hit their top face more often, so you’ll see players split off a tiny die they don’t really need, just to fish for Aura. It still needs an intent, and it still uses one of your splits. That’s smart play, and I’m all for it.

s-intents.title: Intents: What Each Die Is For
s-intents.html: Before you roll, give every die an intent: what it’s trying to do, and who or what it’s aimed at. Say it out loud. This d6 is for the lock. This d4 keeps it quiet. An intent can be anything the story allows: hurt it, disarm it, pin it, shove it off the stairs, grab the key off its belt, find out what it’s hiding. Whatever you gave the die, that’s what happens if it wins.

s-splitting.title: Splitting: shaping your dice
s-splitting.html:
You can split your steps into more, smaller dice. Every action in the roll gives you one split, so one action can turn a d8 into two d4s, or a d2 and a d6. Dice past six steps are already separate and don’t use up your splits, so going past 6 steps gives you a split on top of the one your action gives: 8 steps on one action can be a d6, a d6 and a d4. You can also share your steps out between the dice you’ve got, so a d12 and a d8 can be two d10s.

Your dice all go at things that belong to the same job. A fighter’s steps can disarm, trip and frighten someone, because that’s all part of a fight. If a die would be doing something completely different, like picking a lock in the middle of a sword fight, build it from its own action instead. There’s more on shaping your dice in Tactical Play.

s-going-beyond.title: Going Beyond
s-going-beyond.html:
Every permission, magic or not, does what it says for free, the same as a sword. You need a magic permission or a magic item to do magic at all, and once you’ve got one, it works like anything else.

Going beyond what a permission normally does costs 1 Resolve, for a sword or a spell. It doesn’t add a step. You spend the Resolve and the permission does the bigger thing.

  • Phasing is free until you phase through a wall. That’s 1 Resolve.
  • A master of combat fights for free. An aimed shot that takes out the tag you choose costs 1 Resolve.
  • A necromancer raising the dead to attack or carry something, as part of their own action, is free.
  • Isolde speaks with the recently dead for free. Calling up someone who died a hundred years ago is going beyond, so that’s 1 Resolve.

Anything that works on its own, like a summoned beast or a raised servant acting for you, is summoning, and only a Summoner can do that (see Summoning).

If you have to make a case for why it’s normal, it’s going beyond. Spend the Resolve and keep playing.

s-teamwork.title: Working Together
s-teamwork.html:
There’s no special action for helping. To help a friend, put your action into the same thing they’re doing. That’s a combo: two or more actions going into the same thing at the same time. Add their set actions together and roll once, between you.

  • Nobody pays Aura for it, but it has to be one thing in the story, and you’ve got to be able to join in from where you are. Any number of friends can join one roll.
  • Every action in the roll gives you a split. Your own lines count once, even when the same one’s on two of the set actions you’ve put in. The same permission from two of you counts for each, because you’re two people.
  • Joining a friend’s roll brings your set action’s steps and your action, plus any steps a Leader’s handed you. Whoever rolls gets the Aura for every top face, friends’ dice included.
  • Your own extra action works the same way: bring in another of your set actions as a new approach, like Fight with Sneak for a sneak attack. Put it into the same set action again and it adds 1. Extra actions come from holding your action, spending 1 Resolve, coming out of hiding, cashing in your Confidence when you’re fired up at d12, or a trait or the Boon that says so (see Extra actions).

s-extra-actions.title: Extra actions
s-extra-actions.html:
Now and then you’ll get more than one action in a round:

  • Hold it. Do nothing this round apart from your stride, and you’ve got two actions next round.
  • Spend 1 Resolve for an extra action this round. See Resolve.
  • Come out of hiding. Whoever you are, coming out of hiding gives you an extra action. It’s one extra action, even if you’re Unseen as well.
  • Cash in your Confidence. At d12 you’re fired up, and you can cash it in for an extra action. Your Confidence drops back to d6. See Confidence.
  • A trait that says so. Second Wind gives you one the first time your wound die steps up each scene, and Fast gives you a free Move action in the first round of every scene.
  • The Extra action Boon gives you one extra action a scene. See Boons and Burdens.

An extra action can be its own roll, or it can go into the same roll as a combo. Put it into the same set action again and that’s 1 more step. Put a different set action in and it brings its lines with it as a new approach, like Fight with Sneak for a sneak attack, and anything that’s on both counts once.

s-aura.title: Aura
s-aura.html:
Aura is your character’s luck and flair, the bit of soul they put into a moment when skill alone won’t get them there. It pays for the small stuff.

  • You start every scene full. Your maximum’s 5, unless something on your sheet changes it. A scene is one place and one problem, and the next one starts when that problem’s sorted or the crew moves on. There’s no Aura in downtime.
  • Every top face gives you 1 back, except a summon’s, a die your archetype’s +2 took there, or a number an Oracle swapped in.
  • Already full? Give it to someone else in the scene. Aura’s never wasted while a friend’s nearby.

Spend 1 Aura to:

  • Bring something in that isn’t on your set action, as a step on your roll: one of your own permissions or items, the ground (a chandelier, a crowd, the rain), a threat’s tag you know about (his pride, her greed), a Catch turned your way for a moment, or a friend’s permission through a bond thread you share (see Bonds and threads).
  • Win a tie when you’re the one acting.
  • Intercept for a friend within your stride: take any of the blows aimed at them, and they come at you instead (see Intercept). A Guardian does it for free. Fear, lies and pressure are inside your friend’s head, so nobody can step in front of those.
  • Use your archetype. On most archetypes, 1 Aura adds +2 to one die on its mechanic. Spend it after you roll, once you know you need it. A few get something else for their Aura (see The Archetypes).

1 Aura also keeps a Catch quiet this time, and pays for a quick heal (see Healing).

Traits are free. A trait’s never a step, so there’s nothing to bring in, and it does what its line says every time it applies.

s-resolve.title: Resolve
s-resolve.html:
Resolve is your character pushing themselves, so it pays for the big stuff. You’ve got as much Resolve as you’ve got Titles, so 2 to start, and you can’t hold more than that.

Spend 1 Resolve to:

  • Take an extra action this round, as its own roll or in the same roll as a combo.
  • Roll again. Reroll a roll you just failed, either all your dice or just one, your choice. The threat’s dice stay where they landed. It works in downtime too, where there’s no Aura.
  • Go beyond what a permission normally does (see Going Beyond).
  • Use your archetype’s Resolve spend. Every archetype has one, something big, like a Guardian shrugging off a hit that got through to him (see 1 Resolve on your mechanic).
  • Hold your ground against fear, lies or pressure that gets through, so you don’t drop a size of Confidence. At d2, it saves you the Hurt instead.
  • Act when you’re shaken, with your Confidence down on a d2. It’s 1 Resolve every time you take an action at what the scene’s about.

How Confidence swings during a scene, and what being shaken means, is in Confidence.

Get it back:

  • 1 at the end of every scene, and all of it after downtime.
  • 1 for a big bite, when your Catch or a hostile thread changes the scene or costs you something you wanted. That’s instead of the usual 1 Aura, and it’s your call when (see Catches and Trouble).
  • 1 from the GM for great roleplay, like facing your fear or keeping a promise to yourself.
  • 1 when you strain a bond thread: lean on someone in the story, like calling in a favour or using their name, and the thread’s strained until you mend it (see Bonds and threads).

s-confidence.title: Confidence
s-confidence.html:
Confidence is your nerve, and it’s your defence against fear, lies and pressure. It starts every scene on d6 and moves a size at a time as the scene goes.

  • Up a size for every telegraph your defence stops, whether it’s your Defend or your Confidence, and for every action where one of your dice beats what it was rolled against: a lock opened, a blow landed, a door held, the bell stopped before it rang.
  • Down a size every time your wound die steps up, and for every action where all your dice miss. When your armour or something you carry takes the blow instead, your Confidence doesn’t move.
  • When fear, lies or pressure get through, it drops a size, or you hold your ground for 1 Resolve.
  • At d2 you’re shaken. You can’t take an action at what the scene’s about unless you spend 1 Resolve to do it. Otherwise your action goes on pulling yourself together, and that brings you back up to d4.
  • At d12 you’re fired up. Cash it in for an extra action, or to step your wound die down a size, and it drops back to d6.
  • It never goes below d2 or above d12. When fear, lies or pressure get through and you’re already on d2, it’s a Hurt instead, or 1 Resolve to hold your ground. Anything else that would take it lower leaves it on d2.

When the scene ends, you rest: roll the Confidence you finished on against your wound die, and if you beat it, your wound goes down a size (see Wounds, Blaze and Scars). Then it goes back to d6, so anything that should last past the scene is a Hurt.

s-armour.title: Armour
s-armour.html:
Armour hasn’t got a die of its own. Each piece of plain armour you wear, like worn leathers, a chain shirt, plate or a helmet, is a line on your Defend, a step each, and so is a shield, the way a sword’s a line on Fight. Vesk’s worn leathers make her Defend 2 steps, a d4. Bram’s plate and shield are two lines, and with his first Title and the action, his Defend’s 4 steps, a d8.

When the telegraphs land and you let them ride, you roll your Defend once, and its die stops one blow it beats or ties (see When It Lands). A Defend past 6 steps is more than one die, like any roll, and each of those dice stops one (see Past 6 steps). Spend your action to Defend and every line on it counts twice: Bram’s three lines make 1 + 6 = 7 steps, a d12 and a d2. A condition that says so, like Warded or a spent Poisoned, changes your Defend too (see Conditions to start with).

When a blow gets through, your armour can take it instead. It’s one of the costs you can offer when the GM names a Hurt: not the Hurt, my shield takes it (see Consequences). How many blows a piece can take for you is down to its quality.

s-armour-quality.title: Quality
s-armour-quality.html: Every piece of armour, every shield and every helmet has a quality: Common, Fine or Masterwork. That’s how many boxes it’s got, 1, 2 or 3, and each blow it takes for you ticks one. It’s still a line on your Defend till the last one’s ticked, and then it breaks.

s-defending.title: When It Lands
s-defending.html:
You’re never going to answer everything. Whatever nobody answers lands at the end of the round. If you don’t Defend against it either, you’re letting it ride, and it’s down to your defence, rolled once:

  • Your Defend, rolled once, against the blows, blades, falling rocks and teeth.
  • Your Confidence, rolled once, against the fear, lies, pressure and anything else that works on the mind.

Each die you roll stops one telegraph. Roll them with the telegraphs’ dice, then say which telegraph each of yours stops. It has to beat it or tie it, because ties go to you. Everything else gets through, whatever it rolled, and it costs you something. The GM names what a blow costs you (see Consequences). Fear, lies and pressure cost you a size of Confidence, or 1 Resolve to hold your ground (see When fear gets through).

Your Confidence swings with it. It starts every scene on d6, and from there it moves a size at a time, so keep a token on it.

  • Up a size for every telegraph your defence stops, whether it’s your Defend or your Confidence, and for every action where one of your dice beats what it was rolled against, however many of them won.
  • Down a size every time your wound die steps up, and for every action where all your dice miss. When your armour or something you carry takes the blow instead, it doesn’t move.
  • In a combo, everyone who put an action in moves with the roll, up or down.
  • It stays put on a roll with nothing to beat, like a ward with nothing pushing back, or how far a Move takes you.

At d2 you’re shaken and at d12 you’re fired up, and what both of those do is in Confidence.

s-defend.title: Defend
s-defend.html:
Defend takes your action. When the telegraphs land at the end of the round, every line on your Defend counts twice, and you can split it once. More dice means more telegraphs stopped. Then you choose which die stops which. A condition’s step, like Warded, still counts once.

Your Confidence rolls as it is, because Defending doesn’t make it any bigger. Your Defend’s your dodging, your armour and your shield, and your Confidence is your nerve. Every telegraph your Defend stops still puts your Confidence up a size, the same as when you let it ride, but the Defend itself doesn’t count as a win or a miss on top.

With nothing on your Defend, it’s a d2 either way, so Defending does nothing for you. Answer the blow instead, or get a Guardian in front of it.

It’s what you do when a lot’s coming at you, which is often once you’ve intercepted for your friends. It only covers what lands at the end of the round, though, so a failed answer still lands at once, with no defence roll.

s-intercept.title: Intercept
s-intercept.html:
When a telegraph’s aimed at a friend within your stride, you can step in and intercept it. It costs 1 Aura and no action, and you can do it any time before the telegraphs land. Take as many of the dice aimed at them as you like, from as many enemies as you like, and they come at you instead. Your own defence handles them the usual way, and one die stops one, so if you’ve taken a lot, you’ll want to Defend.

  • One friend for each Aura. Stepping in for two friends is 2 Aura.
  • A Guardian intercepts for free, for every friend within their stride.
  • Only what you can get in front of. You can take a blade or an arrow for a friend, but fear, lies and pressure are inside their head, so nobody can step in front of them. That’s a Bard’s job.
  • The GM’s people can intercept too, without Aura, like the bodyguard who throws himself in front of the knife meant for his lord. She says so before you roll, and your die has to beat his defence instead.
  • A summon intercepts for free, and one hit takes it out (see Summoning).

s-consequences.title: Consequences: When Something Lands
s-consequences.html:
When a telegraph lands on you, or when a miss costs you something because it mattered, a consequence lands. Fear, lies and pressure have their own rule: when they get through, it’s a size of your Confidence or 1 Resolve (see When fear gets through). For everything else, the GM names it from this list, picking one that fits:

  • Take a Hurt. Your wound die goes up a size, and your Confidence drops a size with it. If your wound die’s already a d12, you Blaze. See Wounds, Blaze and Scars.
  • Step your Confidence down one size, for a miss where it fits, like a bluff that falls apart in front of the whole room.
  • Your armour takes it, or something breaks. A piece of armour, a shield or a helmet ticks one of its boxes, and it breaks when the last one’s ticked (see Armour). Anything else you carry just breaks: cross it out until it’s mended. Your attuned things are magic, and they can’t be broken. Your Confidence doesn’t move when something you carry takes it.
  • Step your Aspiration back down one size, never below d2. The blow costs you your dream instead of your body.
  • Step the Party Goal back down one size, never below d2.
  • Tick a clock: step one of the scene’s clocks, or one of the campaign’s, down one.
  • Something else the table agrees fits.

You can offer another. If a different one fits the story and costs about as much, say so, and it lands there instead: not the Hurt, my shield takes it. It has to fit, though: you can’t pay for a blade with your Confidence, and an insult can’t break your shield.

If the telegraph’s intent was something specific, like pin you, grab the painting or knock you off the roof, that’s what happens. You can usually offer a consequence instead: I hold onto the painting and take the blow. The only exception is a telegraph the GM said has only one answer.

s-fear-gets-through.title: When fear gets through
s-fear-gets-through.html:
When fear, lies or pressure get through your Confidence, the GM doesn’t name the cost. For each one that gets through, your Confidence drops a size, or you spend 1 Resolve and hold your ground. It’s your call which.

Nothing takes your Confidence below d2. When fear, lies or pressure get through and you’re already on d2, it’s a Hurt instead, or 1 Resolve to hold your ground. Anything else that would take it lower, like a miss or a Hurt, leaves it on d2.

At d2 you’re shaken. You can’t take an action at what the scene’s about unless you spend 1 Resolve to do it. Otherwise your action goes on pulling yourself together, and that brings you back up to d4.

If a telegraph at your Confidence had a specific intent, like Frightened or Taunted, that’s what happens when it gets through, unless you trade it for a size of your Confidence, or hold your ground for 1 Resolve.

s-blaze.title: Wounds, Blaze and Scars
s-blaze.html:
Your wound die is how hurt you are. It starts at d2, and every Hurt you take puts it up a size: d4, d6, d8, d10, d12. It’s one die for body and mind, so a spear and a night of horrors both put it up. Take a Hurt at d12 and you Blaze.

It’s the die a heal has to beat too, so the worse you’re hurt, the harder you are to patch up. A hit that’s two Hurts, because you were vulnerable, puts it up two sizes, and if that takes it past d12, you Blaze.

Every size your wound die goes up takes your Confidence down a size, so a hit that’s two Hurts costs you two.

s-healing.title: Healing
s-healing.html:
You don’t have to wait for downtime to heal someone, but only a Healer makes a heal roll. It’s an action, built like any other roll from what fits how you’re doing it, and you roll it against your patient’s wound die.

  • Each of your dice that beats it steps it down a size, so split your roll to bring it down further.
  • A heal reaches one person. Split it, and the second die can reach a second person you can touch.
  • Nothing heals anyone below their Scars. With one Scar, a d4’s as far down as they go.

s-vulnerable.title: Vulnerabilities
s-vulnerable.html:
A vulnerability is something that makes a hit hurt more, like Vulnerable to fire, Prone or Opened. Every vulnerability that fits a winning hit adds one more tick, and you choose where each tick goes: another tick off the same tag, or a tick on another of its keeps-it-going tags, which strips a plain one outright. So one vulnerability can strip two plain tags, or take two off one multiplier. It has to make sense, so the hit has to be able to reach what it takes, and nothing under a first tag can go till that tag’s gone. You’ve still got to win, so a miss is a miss.

  • A tick is one Hurt on you, which puts your wound die up a size, or one win off a threat’s tag (see Multipliers).
  • They add up, one each. A goblin that’s Prone, Vulnerable to fire and Vulnerable to blades takes four ticks from a burning sword: one for the hit and three more.
  • The same word never stacks. The same vulnerability twice counts once. Something that’s really weak to fire has two different ones, like Dry as Tinder and Burns Easily.
  • Some are hidden. A hidden vulnerability is a hidden tag, and Study finds it.
  • Two people count twice. Two Warriors who both open the same target are two ticks, because they’re two people.

A vulnerability only adds to a win that’s doing harm: a Hurt, or stripping a tag that keeps a threat going. It doesn’t add to a win that puts a condition on something or moves it. It works the same way on the crew: one vulnerability makes a hit two Hurts, so your wound die goes up two sizes, and your Confidence drops two. Prone and Exposed are the usual ones, and the GM keeps the rest rare on the crew.

s-conditions.title: Conditions
s-conditions.html:
A condition is a tag carrying a die. It can be against you (Burning d8, Pinned d6, Frightened d10) or for you (Warded d8, Unseen d6, Blessed d12). Good or bad, every condition works the same way.

  • Its die is the die that placed it. Beat a Warden with a d10 meant to set it alight, and it’s Burning d10. When nothing pushes back, like a ward on a friend or a blessing before the charge, there’s no roll, and the die you built is the condition’s die (see Wards and blessings).
  • Passive: one step, while it lasts. A condition against you costs you a step on whatever it gets in the way of, and a condition for you gives you a step on whatever it helps. The condition says what fits. It counts once on a roll, however many actions go into it. A few against you make you vulnerable instead, like Prone and Exposed (see Vulnerabilities).
  • Active: spend it for one big thing. Every condition has one strong effect. Spend it and it happens, and the condition’s gone. Spending it doesn’t cost anything: no action, no roll.
  • It fades. At the end of every round, every condition steps down one size, and past d2 it’s gone. It lasts as many rounds as it has steps, so a d4 lasts two and a d12 lasts six.
  • Break it. Spend your action and beat its die: put the fire out, shake off the fear, tear down their ward. A friend can do it for you, if they can reach you.
  • One of each, once a round. Nobody carries two of the same condition, and the same condition goes on the same target only once a round, whoever places it. Spent or broken, it can’t go back on them until next round. Place it again in a later round and the new one replaces the old one, die and all. Different conditions are fine: a Warden can be Burning and Pinned in the same round.

s-bonds.title: Bonds and threads
s-bonds.html:
A bond is usually a person who matters to your character, in the crew or out of it. It can be a faction, a place or a cause too. Each thread is one truth between you, and it’s one of two kinds. A bond thread is something good, like a rescue, a secret you keep for each other or a shared past. A hostile thread is something that’s gone bad, like a debt you can’t pay, a grudge or a betrayal. You can have both kinds with the same person, and as many threads as the story gives you. With no thread at all, you’re neutral.

Each person’s one bond. Write their name once, and every thread you’ve got with them goes under it. A second thread with Dorrie goes under Dorrie, not on a new line with her name on it again.

Any thread can be strained, which means it’s nearly snapped. So a single thread is always one of these: a bond, a bond strained, a hostile thread strained, or hostile, and with no thread you’re neutral.

You start with two bond threads with the crew, from your answers in Connect. Write a hostile thread as well, with anyone, and you’ve got room for a third bond thread. Three bond threads is the most you start with. With two players, one of your two bond threads goes to someone outside the crew, and playing alone, both do.

Every thread’s a hook the GM can pull, and a bond thread’s something you can lean on, too:

  • Borrow through a bond thread. 1 Aura brings one of their permissions into your roll, the same as anything else you bring in, and it doesn’t strain anything. Through a faction, it’s one of its assets. A place or a cause has nothing to lend, but you can still strain a thread with it. You can’t borrow through a strained thread until it’s mended.
  • Strain a bond thread. Lean on them in the story, like calling in the favour, using their name, dragging them into it or using the secret, and take 1 Resolve. It’s free, it doesn’t take an action, and the thread’s now strained.
  • Mend it. Make it right with them, by roleplaying it, doing them a favour or paying them, whatever suits them. That happens in downtime or in a scene with them, not in the middle of the fight where you strained it. Then it’s whole again.
  • Strain it again before it’s mended and it snaps. You still take the Resolve, but cross the thread out. When the last thread goes, so does the bond.

s-trouble.title: Catches and Trouble
s-trouble.html:
A Catch is trouble written on your sheet, ready to go. It comes from an attuned thing (see Attunement), or from a Scar, the wound you keep after you Blaze (see Wounds, Blaze and Scars). It’s got to be something that can bring real trouble into a scene, something the GM can run with. If it’d never come up, it isn’t a Catch.

Trouble’s yours to bring. Letting your Catches bite is up to you, and the GM doesn’t hand out trouble. She makes things go wrong in all the usual ways, like telegraphs and the cost of a miss.

  • Let it bite, as often as you like. Say how it causes trouble, the GM runs with it, and you take 1 Aura. Every bite has to bring real trouble.
  • A big bite changes the scene or costs you something you wanted. Take 1 Resolve for it instead of the Aura. It’s your call when.
  • A hostile thread bites the same way as a Catch, for 1 Aura, or 1 Resolve for a big bite (see Bonds and threads).
  • No Catch? Bring real trouble on yourself in the story anyway, and take 1 Aura.

s-aspiration.title: Aspiration
s-aspiration.html:
Your Aspiration is one thing you want. It starts at d2 and climbs as you chase it, so the first steps come easy and the last ones are hard work. The crew writes its Party Goal at d2 as well, and it climbs the same way.

  • Chase it. When something you do really moves it along, roll against its die, built from whatever you’re doing about it. Beat it and it climbs one. In a scene, that’s an action aimed at it, when the GM says it’s within reach (usually once or twice a session). In downtime, it’s a slot.
  • One step a roll. However many dice you put on it, one roll moves it one step at most. More dice is advantage, and your best die counts.
  • A setback steps it back down one, never below d2.

When it climbs past d12, it resolves: you get what you were after, and you take a new archetype with one permission, name it with a Title, and write a new Aspiration at d2. Another Title puts your Resolve maximum up by 1 as well.

Your Aspiration is also somewhere a consequence can land. When a blow or a failure costs you, you can step your Aspiration back down instead of taking it on your body or your gear, so the fight costs you your dream instead of your skin. You can’t do it while it’s at d2.

s-good-aspiration.title: A good Aspiration
s-good-aspiration.html:
When your Aspiration climbs past d12, you get what you wrote, so make it something you could have in an arc or two. Vesk’s first one took her seven sessions. A good one passes all four of these:

  • It’s one thing. Wren has to find the thing before she can put it down, and Ash will either burn the Ember Court down or take it back, but each of them is after one thing. If you want two things, write the first, and the other can be your next Aspiration.
  • You’d know the day it’s done. There’s a moment you could point at, like Vesk walking out of the vault or Bram getting his rank back. Be rich hasn’t got one, so when it climbs past d12, nobody knows what you’ve got.
  • It’s about someone or something in the world. That’s what lets the GM put it within reach. Dorrie’s Get a seat at the table that ruined my family points at the people who did it, so the GM knows who to put in her way.
  • The story goes on after it. You get it, and then everyone else gets to react. Never get caught again would mean nothing could ever catch Vesk, so leave out words like never and can’t.

Each of these has a version that’s too big or too vague, then what the crew wrote:

  • Be the best thief there’s ever been has no day it’s done. Own the score of a lifetime is one job, and Vesk will know it when she’s pulled it.
  • Be a hero again could mean anything. Earn back the rank they stripped from me says what Bram’s after and who has to give it back.
  • Bring my order back is a whole campaign. Find out who burned my order’s library is where Isolde starts.
  • Kill the thing that took my brother and make sure it never happens again is two things, and the second one never ends. Find the thing that took my brother, and put it down keeps the first.

If yours is too big or too vague, the GM says so, and you work it out together before it goes on your sheet. Usually that means keeping the first piece of it, and the rest makes a good next Aspiration for when this one resolves.

how-permissions-stack.title: How permissions stack
how-permissions-stack.html:
Every line that fits what you’re doing is a step, and it counts once a roll.

  • A permission goes on two set actions at most, and Defend counts as one. Put each one on the two where it’ll help most. Anywhere else, it’s 1 Aura to bring in, the same as anything that isn’t on your set action.
  • Titles go on every set action they fit. There’s no cap on Titles.
  • A plain item goes on one set action, the one where it’ll help most. Anywhere else, it’s 1 Aura to bring in.
  • The same word never counts twice. You can take a permission more than once, on either Title, and each copy goes on two set actions of its own, but the same permission can’t sit on one set action twice. To stack, use different words: Deceptive and Sly can both sit on your Fight. Fight two at once and fight in tight spaces are two different permissions, so they’re fine together.
  • In a combo, each of you counts on your own. Your Deceptive and Dorrie’s are both steps, because they’re two people.
  • Permissions don’t come in levels. One you picked up last week is worth the same 1 step as one you started with.

your-slots.title: Your Slots
your-slots.html:
Every player gets two personal slots, or three with Tireless. The crew gets one action, the same as every faction on the board, and nothing buys it another. Put one of your personal slots into the crew’s action and everything counts twice. A personal slot can also chase the Goal, work a project or support an Aspiration on its own, but it can never be a second move on a faction.

Two things happen without costing a slot: when downtime’s over, all your Resolve comes back and your wound die goes back to d2, or to your Scars. A trait that fires every downtime, like Host or Cache, does it by itself.

s-downtime-rolls.title: Rolling in downtime
s-downtime-rolls.html:
Most slots just happen. When something pushes back (the fence wants his money, or the Guild’s watching the smithy), roll for it like any Challenge.

  • Ties go to the defender, every time. A die you’re climbing counts as the defender.
  • There’s no Aura in downtime, so you can’t pay to win a tie. You’ve got two other ways out: spend 1 Resolve to roll again (your dice only), or spend one of the crew’s extra resources and take the tie. It’s the crew’s money, so ask the table first.
  • Only the crew can do that. A faction never rerolls, and never buys a tie.

s-goal.title: The Party Goal
s-goal.html:
The Goal is what the crew’s after this arc, like clear Dorrie’s name, free the Bound or own the Low Market. It starts at d2 and climbs.

  • It climbs when someone chases it and wins: an action in a scene when the GM says the Goal’s within reach, or in downtime, the crew’s action or a personal slot someone puts toward it.
  • It steps back down one when a consequence lands on it, or when the crew takes a real setback. It never goes below d2.
  • When it climbs past d12, the crew’s done it. Play the moment out. Then the crew grows (see How the crew grows), everyone writes one new thread, to someone the Goal brought into their life, and the table writes the next Goal, at d2.

s-good-goal.title: A good Goal
s-good-goal.html:
When the Goal climbs past d12, the crew’s done it, and they get whatever it says. So write one they can get done in one arc, and make it something the whole crew wants. Everything that makes a good Aspiration makes a good Goal too: it’s one thing, you’d know the day it’s done, it’s about someone or something in the world, and the story goes on after it.

  • Rule the city is a whole campaign. Own the Low Market is one arc of it.
  • Keep the harbour safe never ends. Clear Dorrie’s name is done the day she wins in court.
  • Bring peace to the Steeplands, with treaties nobody can break is every city at once, and it’s meant to last forever. Get the Harbour Guild and the Vane Estate to sign a truce fits in an arc, and whether the truce holds is the next story.

A Goal that’s too big is usually where the campaign’s heading. Say it out loud so the GM can build toward it, and make its first piece the Goal. If the table writes one that’s too big or too vague, the GM says so, and you work it out together before it goes on the party sheet.

s-climb.title: Things That Climb
s-climb.html:
Most dice in Zi’Dara count down. A scene clock, a stake clock, an event, Supplies and the alarm all step down, and past d2, whatever they were counting to happens. Four things on the party sheet count up instead: the Goal, every Aspiration, every project and every faction’s agenda. They start low and climb as someone works at them, so the first steps come easy and the last ones are hard work.

Roll against its die. Beat it and it climbs one. Past d12, it’s done. One roll moves it one step at most, so more dice on it is advantage, and your best die counts. A setback steps it down one, but never below d2.

  • In a scene, an action aimed at it rolls against its die, when the GM says it’s within reach. That’s usually once or twice a session, when a scene’s really about it.
  • In downtime, the crew’s action or a personal slot spent on it is one roll.
  • Whoever does it builds the roll. In a scene it’s an action like any other, built from the set action that fits. In downtime it’s 1 step for the crew’s action or the slot, plus everything on their sheet that fits what they’re doing about it.
  • Ties go to the die you’re climbing. In a scene you can pay 1 Aura to win one, the same as always. In downtime there’s no Aura, so see Rolling in downtime.

s-projects.title: Projects
s-projects.html:
A project is anything the crew, or one of them, sets out to build or bring about over time: a ring of informants in the Low Market, a forged charter, a ship refitted, the salt carters turned against the Vane Estate. Write one line for what it is, and one for what happens when it’s done.

  • It starts at d2, like the Goal. If the crew’s already partway there, start it higher: a d6, or a d10 when one more push would do it.
  • Work it the same way. An action that chases it when it’s within reach, or in downtime the crew’s action or a personal slot, rolls against its die.
  • Past d12, it’s done, and what you wrote happens.
  • Keep two or three on the go, at most. Any more and none of them gets anywhere.

Projects are how a small crew takes on a big faction. You can’t go straight at the Vane Estate’s Power without the crew’s action and a personal slot on the same move (see Factions), but you can start Turn the salt carters against the Estate, and write that when it’s done, the Estate loses its Salt Contracts. The crew’s action can work it, and so can anyone’s personal slot, and every roll at it is one the Estate doesn’t see coming.

s-crew-size.title: How big it is
s-crew-size.html: The die’s 1 step, plus the assets that add Power, so a crew with Muscle as well as its back room is a d6.

s-crew-tags.title: Crew Assets
s-crew-tags.html: Here are twelve to pick from. There are plenty more in Appendix B, for the crew or any faction, or you can write your own in the same shape. Each one needs a resource paying for it, like any asset, and does exactly what it says.

s-crew-wealth.title: Extra Resources
s-crew-wealth.html:
An extra resource is one that isn’t paying for an asset. It’s spent each downtime, not saved, so each one buys one of these between one downtime and the next:

  • A new asset of the crew’s own. It takes the crew’s action to build (that’s Establish), and the extra resource pays for it from then on.
  • Another faction’s action. Pay a faction and it spends its one action that downtime where the crew says, rolled with its own dice. A faction that’s hostile to the crew won’t take its money, and the money buys the action, not the win.
  • An asset or a resource from a faction that’ll sell, which means one that isn’t hostile to the crew. It changes hands, and an asset needs a resource paying for it from then on.
  • A tie won on a downtime roll (see Rolling in downtime).
  • Anything too big for a purse, in a session: passage for twenty, a house, a magistrate’s goodwill. When the money’s what does it, it counts as a permission on the roll.

It can’t buy the crew another action. The crew gets one a downtime, like every faction, and nothing buys any faction more than that.

s-crew-grows.title: How the crew grows
s-crew-grows.html:
• When the Goal’s done, the crew earns a new Reputation and picks two of these: a new resource, a new asset (it’ll need something to pay for it), or a new holding.
  • When it takes something big (a building, a ship, a street) or a faction it’s been fighting falls, it picks one.
  • A big job can pay a resource. When it will, the GM says so when she offers it.
  • It shrinks when a faction takes or destroys its assets or resources.
  • Rebuild with the crew’s action. That’s Establish, and it brings back an asset or a resource the crew’s lost. An asset still needs something paying for it.
  • A brand-new resource comes from the Goal, a big job or a project, or off a faction, by Acquiring it or buying it with an extra resource. Establish only builds back one the crew’s lost.
  • Its action is its turn. The crew doesn’t take a faction turn on top of its one action a downtime.

There’s a whole campaign of it, from a crew with no name to a power in the Low Market, in The Crew, Session 1 to 20.

s-party-resources.title: Party Holdings
s-party-resources.html: Big things, like a horse, a cart, a small boat or a house, are party holdings rather than items. The story decides whether you’ve got access to them, and the crew keeps track of them together. A holding counts as a line on any roll it fits for whoever’s using it: a fast horse in a chase, or a safehouse when the crew needs to disappear. It isn’t on anyone’s set action, so bringing it into a roll costs 1 Aura, the same as bringing in the ground. A holding isn’t an asset, so nothing has to pay for it.

s-faction-board.title: What a Faction Is
s-faction-board.html:
You write a faction once, and from then on its card does the work. Take your time building it, the way you would a character, because after that it runs on one action a downtime. A faction’s card has its name and nine lines:

  • Power: its die. It’s 1 step, plus 1 for each lot of people who’ll turn up when it calls, so one army makes a d4 and five lots of people make a d12. Nothing else adds Power: a charter or an old name is an asset that does one thing. It’s what the faction rolls when it acts and what it defends with. Leave out an asset that doesn’t fit what it’s doing, the same as a line on a set action: a navy doesn’t help in the mountains. Its best people are threats with a Challenge to match, so a d8 Power sends Challenge 4, and its face can go higher than that.
  • Resources: permissions for where its money comes from, one line each, like Silver Mine, Grain Fields or Harbour Tolls.
  • Assets: permissions for what it can do, one line each, and every one says exactly what it does: Standing Army (+1 Power), Spy Network (once a downtime, ask the GM one question about another faction), Deep-Water Docks (it can trade with anyone across the sea). Don’t read in anything an asset doesn’t say. Big ones carry a multiplier, like Standing Army ×3, and take that many wins to destroy or to take.
  • Want: one sentence, the thing it always wants.
  • Agenda: what it’s doing right now, on a die that climbs as the faction works at it. The die says how close it is, and once it’s past d12, it happens (see Agendas).
  • Face: the person the crew deals with, written as a threat.
  • Secret: one hidden tag, and usually its weakness.
  • Bonds: Public Sentiment, Morale and Loyalty, with their threads (see Bonds).
  • Threads: its bond and hostile threads toward the crew, and toward other factions when they matter (see How a Faction Sees the Crew).

s-wealth.title: Resources and Assets
s-wealth.html:
Every asset needs one resource paying for it, every downtime. Count them when you build the faction, and again whenever something’s taken, broken, built or bought. Nothing else needs counting.

  • An asset with nothing paying for it stops counting till something does: no Power and no effect. The faction picks which one goes unpaid. That’s how the crew pulls a faction down: burn the mine, and the army it paid for stops counting.
  • An extra resource, one that isn’t paying for anything, is spent each downtime, not saved. It can hire another faction: that faction spends its one action that downtime where the payer says, rolled with its own dice, and the payer still takes its own. It can pay for a new asset, or it can go into a trade.
  • Hiring needs a willing faction. A faction that’s hostile to the payer, with mostly hostile threads toward it, won’t take its money, and the money buys the action, not the win.
  • Building an asset is Establish: the faction’s action, and an extra resource to pay for it. Dismantling one frees its resource. Selling one moves it to the buyer, for whatever they agree. Trades between factions are agreed in the story and cost no action.
  • Big deals can be paid over a few downtimes or shipped along a trade route, and then they can be stolen or stopped on the way. Only bother when the crew’s involved or it makes a story.

s-faction-bonds.title: Bonds
s-faction-bonds.html:
Every faction has three bonds, and each one asks a different question:

  • Public Sentiment: what do the people it rules or serves think of it?
  • Morale: will its own people keep going when it gets hard?
  • Loyalty: will they stand by it, or turn?

Each bond holds threads, one fact each, like a character’s: The Crown protected our village from famine. They come in the same two kinds, too. A bond thread is good for the faction, and a hostile thread is something that’s gone bad for it.

  • A bond thread is a step on any roll it fits.
  • A hostile thread is a vulnerability. Every hit that fits it ticks once more: when a Destroy or an Acquire wins against the faction, each hostile thread that fits adds a tick.
  • A strained thread stops counting till it’s mended, and straining it again snaps it.
  • No thread at all is neutral, so don’t write one till something happens.

The Vane Estate’s Loyalty thread is a hostile one: The guard’s been on the same pay for twenty years. Say a Destroy wins against its Household Guard ×2 by talking the guard into walking out. That thread fits, so the win ticks twice, and the guard’s gone in one.

When you write them:

s-agendas.title: Agendas
s-agendas.html: An agenda climbs, like the crew’s Goal, and its die tells you how close it is. A d2 has only just started, and it’s years off. A d4 is a season or more away, a d6 a month or two, a d8 a week or two, a d10 is days away, and a d12 could happen any day now. Past d12, it happens. A faction can have two agendas on the go at once, but never more than two.

when-an-agenda-happens.title: When an agenda happens
when-an-agenda-happens.html:
• The world changes. Say how in one sentence, and write it on the party sheet.
  • The faction grows. Give it a new asset or a new resource. A new asset needs something paying for it, like any other.
  • It writes a new agenda. Roll for it, or pick what it wants next.

s-standing.title: How a Faction Sees the Crew
s-standing.html:
Factions have threads toward each other and toward the crew, one fact each, like They brought our ledgers up from the sunk barge. Each one’s a bond thread or a hostile thread, the same as a character’s. They’re one-way: the Guild’s thread toward the Estate isn’t the Estate’s toward the Guild. Write them as things happen.

How a faction sees the crew is its threads toward them:

  • Mostly bond threads, and it’s friendly. It helps when it costs little, and it asks favours.
  • None, or as many hostile as bond, and it does business. Everything has a price.
  • Mostly hostile threads, and it’s hostile. It watches, and it’ll hurt the crew when it’s cheap to.

A real service writes a bond thread: a job done well, a gift, a favour returned, or one of its enemies brought down. Costing it something it cares about writes a hostile one, like an asset, a resource, or its face humiliated. A betrayal snaps every bond thread it has toward the crew.

Most factions start with none. If the crew’s already crossed one, write that as a hostile thread.

These threads aren’t in its bonds. A bond thread’s a step for the crew on any roll it fits, and a hostile one doesn’t add a tick to anything. A strained thread doesn’t count for anything till it’s whole again.

s-mini-factions.title: Mini Factions
s-mini-factions.html:
A core faction can make up to three mini factions: a smuggling crew the Guild runs, a company it hired for good, a cell inside the watch. A mini faction’s less to run, and it puts more on the board. Mini factions don’t count toward the four to twelve, and the crew can make them too, the same way.

  • Making one is Establish: the parent’s action, and the parent hands over one of its own resources and one of its own assets. They’re the mini faction’s now, so it costs twice what building an asset does.
  • A new mini faction doesn’t act in the downtime it’s made. From the next one on, it takes its own action like any faction, and it’s got a mind of its own: at first it mostly does what its parent wants, then it starts going its own way, and other factions can work on it too.
  • It picks two of the six outcomes, and those are the only things it can do.
  • Its card’s short: its name, its Power (1 step, plus 1 if its asset adds Power), its resource and its asset, its two outcomes, and its Loyalty thread toward the parent.
  • It can’t make mini factions, and its Power doesn’t add to its parent’s.
  • Loyalty isn’t obedience. The parent can order it, pay it, threaten it or talk it round, and none of it’s guaranteed. Its Loyalty thread is one the crew can strain, so turning a faction’s mini faction is a job worth taking.

Say the Harbour Guild makes The Night Boats, a smuggling crew. It hands over Dock Fees, one of its resources, and Fast Boats, an asset that adds Power, so the Guild’s own Power drops a step, from a d10 to a d8. The Night Boats sit out this downtime. From the next one they take their own action, and to start with, they’ll mostly run whatever the Guild wants run.

s-faction-build.title: Building a Faction
s-faction-build.html: Roll on each table, or just read down them and pick.

s-faction-turn.title: The Faction Turn
s-faction-turn.html:
Every downtime, every faction on the board takes one action, and only one: each core faction, each mini faction, and the crew. Nothing buys a faction a second one. The only faction that doesn’t act is a mini faction in the downtime it’s made (see Mini Factions). It works like a telegraph:

  1. At the start of downtime, the GM telegraphs every faction’s action: what it’s doing, who or what it’s aimed at, and its dice. Whichever one matters most to the crew is the faction pressure. With a big board, only telegraph the factions the crew can reach, and let the rest move off-screen: say what changed, with no roll.
  2. The crew takes its action, and everyone spends their personal slots. The crew can move against a faction before that faction’s action lands.
  3. Then the actions land. Roll them.

Hiring comes first. Before she telegraphs, the crew says who it’s paying with an extra resource, and she decides who the factions are paying. A hired faction spends its one action on the job, and its telegraph is the job it was paid for, so once the actions are on the table, nobody can buy one off.

  • Its roll is its Power, plus a step for each bond thread that fits (see Bonds). One action gives it one split, so it can go for two things in the same job, and each die’s its own outcome: take the shipment, and keep its name out of it. One can land and the other miss.
  • What it rolls against is another faction’s Power, rolled once the first time anyone goes at it that downtime, so everyone who goes at it after that has to beat the same roll, the same as a threat. Or it’s the die of whatever it’s after: its agenda, a stake, a person. Ties go to the defender, and a die it’s climbing counts as the defender. If it loses, nothing happens this downtime, and it’s a little angrier about it.
  • An action is one of the six outcomes, or work on its agenda: its Power against the agenda’s die, and beat it and it climbs one. Writing a new agenda takes its action too, and a faction can have two at once, never more. Coming for the crew takes its action as well (see When a Faction Comes for the Crew).
  • Some actions don’t need a roll, like writing a new agenda, or Establishing with nobody in the way. They happen, unless someone Obstructs them.

s-faction-outcomes.title: The Six Outcomes
s-faction-outcomes.html: Each outcome changes one thing on a card.

s-faction-comes.title: When a Faction Comes for the Crew
s-faction-comes.html:
When a faction’s action is coming for the crew, roll a d12 as you telegraph it, so the crew knows what’s coming. A faction whose threads toward the crew are mostly hostile rolls on the first table, and one whose threads are mostly bond threads rolls on the second. One with none, or as many bond as hostile, rolls a d2 first: on a 1 it uses the first table, and on a 2 it uses the second.

It doesn’t roll against the crew. Whatever comes up happens, unless the crew Obstructs it. When a faction’s been paid to come for the crew, roll on the table for the payer’s threads toward the crew, not its own.

s-faction-crew.title: The Crew and the Factions
s-faction-crew.html:
The crew’s a faction too, on the same card (see The Party Sheet), so it takes one action a downtime, the same as every other faction. Roll the crew’s Power, plus a step for every Reputation and bond thread that fits: when the crew goes to the Guildmaster for a favour, the Guild’s bond thread toward them is a step. If one character’s plainly the right person for it, they can roll their own permissions instead: 1 step for the action, plus everything that fits.

A player can put one of their personal slots into the crew’s action, and two slots on one move count everything twice. A personal slot can never be a second move on a faction, though, and nothing buys the crew another action (see Downtime).

Going at a bigger faction. If a faction’s Power is bigger than the crew’s, the crew can only roll against its Power with two slots on that one move: the crew’s action, and a personal slot put into it. That goes for Obstructing its action too, since its dice are its Power. With the crew’s action on its own, go at the smaller things: one asset or resource that’s out on its own, its agenda, its face, its people, or a project of your own that’ll cost it something when it’s done.

An asset or a resource that’s out on its own, like a warehouse on the docks or vineyards up in the hills, only has what’s guarding it: 1 step, plus each asset that adds Power and is really there. It rolls its own die. The Estate’s Power is a d12, so the crew’s action on its own can’t touch it, but only its Hired Swords ride out to the vineyards. That’s 1 step plus the swords, 2 steps, a d4, and the crew’s d4 can go at that with its action alone.

The crew’s moves are the six outcomes, the same as any faction’s, plus two of its own.

party-slots.title: The crew’s action
party-slots.html:
The crew’s action is its one move a downtime, and it can be any of these. When someone puts a personal slot into it as well, that’s two slots on one thing, and everything counts twice.

  • Chase the Goal. Whoever does it rolls against the Goal’s die: 1 step for the action, plus everything of theirs that fits. Beat it and it climbs one. See The Party Goal.
  • Work a project. The same, against the project’s die. See Projects.
  • Move on a faction. Destroy, Undermine, Obstruct, Influence, Acquire or Establish, set back its agenda, or work for it. See Factions.
  • Rebuild. Establish an asset or a resource the crew’s lost. An asset still needs a resource paying for it. See How the crew grows.
  • Advance a world event. Push something along, or hold it back.
  • Support an Aspiration. One more roll at someone’s Aspiration, built by whoever’s helping.

A personal slot that chases the Goal, works a project or supports an Aspiration on its own rolls the same way, with 1 step for the slot. Something that climbs still only climbs one step a roll, however many slots went into it.
